activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: On your birthday, you turn one year older.
story:
Hunter ran into the big hall. Balloons hung from the ceiling. Grandma had tied them there.

A long table stood by the window. On it was a cake with four candles. Dad used a match to light them. Hunter watched from his chair. He did not touch the matches.

"I was three yesterday," Hunter said. "Am I still three?"

"Blow out your candles," said Mom. "Then you will see."

Hunter stood up. He was careful not to lean too far. He took a big breath. He blew hard. All four candles went out. The smoke curled up like a little feather.

"Now count them," said Grandma.

Hunter touched the candles one by one. "One, two, three, four."

"You are four today," said Mom.

Hunter jumped up and down. "I got bigger!" he said. "Watch me blow again next year!"

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Seeds need water to start growing.
story:
Alexander had a new patch of dirt in the backyard. He poked little holes with his finger. He dropped a carrot seed in each hole. Then he patted the dirt down flat.

Every morning Alexander ran outside. He looked and looked. The dirt stayed brown and smooth. Nothing was happening. "Where are my carrots?" he asked.

Dad sat on the swing nearby. "Did you give the seeds a drink?" he asked. Alexander shook his head. He ran to get his little green watering can. He tipped it over the dirt. Water made dark round spots on the soil.

The next morning, something green peeked up. Then he saw a tiny worm stick out its tongue-less face, and behind it, another sprout, and another. Alexander laughed. He filled the watering can all the way to the top.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Birds are animals that have feathers.
story:
Iris wanted to find her toy robot. It was lost somewhere at home. She looked under the table. She looked in her toy box. No robot there.

Then Iris went to the backyard with Dad. The grass was cool and soft. Something white lay in the grass. It was light and soft like a little fan. Iris picked it up. "A feather!" she said. Birds have feathers. So a bird must have been here. She looked up. A small bird sat on the fence. It chirped at her.

Iris wiped the feather with her fingers. She wanted to give it back. She set the feather on the bird bath. The bird hopped down near it. Then Iris heard a beep, beep. Her robot was in the flower pot by the door! She hugged it tight. "Found you," she said.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Two people can feel differently about the same thing.
story:
Alexis went to the park with his drum. Bang, bang, bang! The drum was loud and fun. Alexis felt excited. He played a happy beat. He counted his hits. One, two, three!

His friend Mia came to play. Mia put her hands on her ears. "Too loud," she said. Her face looked sad and a little scared. She hid behind the big tree.

Alexis stopped drumming. He felt angry for a tiny moment. He wanted to drum more! But then he looked at Mia. She did not like the loud drum. He liked the loud drum. Same drum, different feelings. Hmm.

"Let's play quiet," said Alexis. He put the drum down. They found a cozy spot under a leafy bush. It was like a little green house. Alexis put leaves on a plate he found in the sand toys. "Leaf cake!" he said. Mia clapped softly. "Yum!" she said. Alexis patted the drum very gently. Tap, tap. Mia smiled. Alexis smiled too. "Quiet drum," said Mia. Tap, tap, tap.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange paint.
story:
Norah sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a big pumpkin. But there was no orange paint. "Where did the orange go?" she asked. Her teacher, Miss Kim, said, "Maybe you can find out."

Norah looked at the cups. Red paint. Blue paint. Yellow paint. Green paint. No orange at all. Sam sat next to her. He was painting a green frog. "Watch this," Sam said. He put a brush in the red cup. Then he put red in the yellow cup. He stirred it round and round.

The yellow turned orange! Norah clapped her hands. "Can I try?" she asked. "Yes," said Sam. Norah dipped her brush in the red paint. She stirred it into the yellow. Swish, swish. The paint got darker. Now it was orange, just like a real pumpkin. It smelled a little stinky, like all paints do. "Can I pay you back with my yellow?" Norah asked. Sam laughed. "You can just share it." Miss Kim came over and smiled. She stuck a magnet on the wall and hung the wet painting up high. "It will dry there," she said. Norah looked up at her orange pumpkin and smiled. "I made orange all by myself," she said.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A rectangle has four sides and four square corners, like the shape of a door.
story:
Theodore ran to art class. "Today we paint shapes!" said Miss Amy. She held up a red bucket of brushes. Theodore grabbed one fast. He wanted to paint a big house.

First he painted a square. Four sides, flat like a box. Then he painted a triangle on top. Pointy like a hat! "The house needs a door," said Theodore. He looked around the room. What shape was a door?

He ran to the real door and looked. He touched one corner. Then another. "One, two, three, four," he counted. Four corners! The door was a rectangle. A rectangle has four sides and four square corners, just like this door. Theodore laughed out loud.

He ran back to his paint. He painted a rectangle door on his square house. He painted tiny circle windows too. "Look, Miss Amy!" he said. "My door is a rectangle, like the real one!" Miss Amy clapped her hands. Theodore spelled out the word D-O-O-R at the bottom. Then he held his painting up high for everyone to see.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: We hear with our ears.
story:
William sat very still on the back step. His ears heard a bird singing. "What do I hear with?" he asked himself. "My ears!" Then he heard a bee buzz. Ears again.

He touched a smooth, clean stone. "I feel with my hands," he said. He sniffed a red flower. "I smell with my nose." He popped a tiny seed in his mouth. "No, no," said Grandma. "Seeds are for planting, not eating." William put the seed in the dirt instead.

A dog barked next door. William's ears heard it. He put his hands over his ears. The bark got small and quiet. He took his hands off. The bark got big again. "My ears hear the dog," said William. He listened until the dog went quiet too. Then Grandma called, "William, cookie time!" William heard her with his ears and ran.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil point can break if you press down very hard.
story:
Myles sat at the little table in the art room. He wanted to draw a big furry dog for his mom. He picked up his pencil and started to draw. He pressed down very hard. He wanted the dog to be dark and easy to see.

Then something happened. Snap! The pencil point broke off. The little piece fell onto the table. Myles picked it up and looked at it. He turned the pencil around in his hand. Would a soft press work too?

He got a new pencil from the jar. This time he pressed gently. The line was soft and gray. He pressed a little more, still gently. The line got darker. The pencil point stayed on. Myles smiled. He drew the furry dog, stroke by stroke, soft and slow.

At the end of class, the drawings hung on a string with clips. His furry dog swung a little when the teacher walked by. Myles pointed at it. "Look at my dog!" he said. "I pressed soft, so the point stayed on."

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: Taking slow, deep breaths can help you feel calmer when you are scared.
story:
Jake was at home with his teddy bear. Today he had to get a shot at the doctor. His tummy felt funny. "Will it hurt?" he asked Grandpa. "Just a tiny pinch," said Grandpa. "Then it is done."

In the waiting room, Jake held his teddy tight. A cute baby sat on his mom's lap nearby. Jake's feet did not stop wiggling. He did not want his turn to come.

Grandpa sat down next to him. "Smell the flower," Grandpa said. He held up his hand like a flower. Jake breathed in slow. "Now blow out the birthday candle," said Grandpa. Jake blew out slow. They did it again. One, smell the flower. Two, blow the candle. Three, smell the flower. Jake's feet stopped wiggling.

"Jake," the nurse called. Jake walked in all by himself. He smelled the flower. He blew the candle. The nurse said, "All done!" It was just a tiny pinch, and it was over.

At home, Jake got a sticker and a hug. Then he gave his teddy a pretend shot. "Smell the flower, teddy," he said. At lunch, Jake used his fork to feed himself bite by bite. He felt big. After lunch, he told teddy, "You were brave too."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Soon means in a little while.
story:
Athena went to the store with Mom. Today Athena wanted pink strawberries. Yesterday the store had none. "Maybe today," said Mom.

Athena looked at the fruit bins. She saw apples. She saw bananas. No strawberries yet. "The truck comes soon," said the fruit man. "Soon means a little wait," Mom said with a smile. Athena did not like waiting.

Then Athena heard a big noise outside. A bus stopped by the store. Men carried boxes off the bus. The boxes went into the store. Athena watched. One box had pink on it. The fruit man opened it. Strawberries!

"Can we get some now?" asked Athena. "Yes, now," said Mom. She let Athena pick the box. Athena held it all the way to the pay desk.

At home, Mom washed the berries. Athena ate three. They were sweet. "Can we buy more tomorrow?" she asked. "Tomorrow, yes," said Mom. Athena jumped up and down. "The truck came soon, just like the man said!" she said. Mom clapped and showed Athena one big berry. "This one is for you," said Mom.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: The small pictures on a tablet screen are called icons, and tapping one opens an app.
story:
Lennon went to the library with her dad. She saw a tablet on the little table. She wanted to draw a cat on it.

The screen was dark. Dad showed her the small round button. She pushed it. The screen lit up. "I did it!" she said.

Now she wanted to draw. She looked at the screen. It had lots of small pictures. She saw a paintbrush picture. She tapped it with one finger. The drawing app opened. There was a big white page, just like a cloud.

Lennon drew a cat with a long tail. Then she drew a sun. A boy sat down next to her. He was noisy because he wanted a turn too. Lennon drew him a little dog. He smiled.

The librarian said time was up. Lennon did not cry. She pushed the button and the screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the table. "Bye bye, tablet," she said.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: After using the toilet, we flush and then wash our hands.
story:
Rowan sat at the dinner table. He had a warm bowl of soup. He took a big sip. Then he wiggled in his seat. "I need to go potty," he said. He ran down the hall.

Rowan used the toilet. He pulled up his pants. He washed his hands. He heard the sink go whoosh. The water felt cool on his fingers. Then he ran back to the table.

Mama was looking at him. "Did you flush?" she asked. Rowan thought hard. Had he flushed? He did not think so. He ran back down the hall. He pushed the little silver handle. Whoosh! The water swirled down. Then he washed his hands again, just to be sure. The soap smelled like flowers.

Back at the table, his soup was still warm. He patted his tummy. "All done with potty," he said. "Flush and wash. Flush and wash." Mama laughed. "That's right, Rowan." Rowan ate his soup. His toes were cozy in his red sock. Soon his eyes felt sleepy. After dinner came a bath, then pajamas. Rowan smiled. Tomorrow he would flush and wash all by himself again.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: A pretend tea party can use empty cups with no real tea in them.
story:
Ayla went to the park with her grandma. She brought her bunny and her bear. She wanted to play tea party. But she had no real teacups.

Ayla looked in the toy box by the sandbox. There was one red cup. It was empty. No water, no tea. She felt sad. Her bunny was thirsty!

Then Ayla had an idea. She held the cup over her bear. She tipped it slowly. "More tea?" she asked. Nothing came out. She poured it again anyway.

"Drink up, bear!" she said. Bear drank and drank. "That was yummy tea," said grandma in a big bear voice. Ayla giggled. Her cup had no tea in it at all. But bear liked it anyway!

Ayla gave bunny a cup too. She poured and poured. "Careful," she said. "It is pretend hot!" Bunny sipped very slowly. Bunny blew on it. "Too hot, bunny?" asked Ayla. Bunny nodded. Ayla waited and counted to three.

Then she set the cups on a little bench. She wrapped bunny in her jacket. "Now bunny is cozy," she said. The wind came. It blew a leaf into the red cup.

"Oh no!" said Ayla. "The wind wants tea too!" Grandma laughed and clapped. Ayla tipped the leaf out. She poured one more cup, just for the wind.

"Last cup," said Ayla. She held it up high. "Tea time for everyone!" she said.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many celebrations have special foods made just for that day.
story:
Grandma came early with a big box. It was time for the family party. Inside the box were dates and honey and flour. "We make these sweets only on this day," said Grandma. Felix wanted to taste one now.

"Can I have one?" he asked. "Not yet," said Grandma. "First we mix, then we bake, then we wait." Felix helped from his chair. He poured the flour. It went poof on his nose. Grandma laughed. "Now you look like a snowy cat," she said.

The oven was hot, so Grandma put the pan in. Felix watched through the little window. The little dough balls got big and brown. When they came out, Felix was sleepy. But he woke up fast. He lifted a warm sweet from the plate. He took one big bite. "It tastes like honey and sunshine," he said. Grandma smiled and took a bite too.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: A hairdresser uses a comb to keep hair neat while cutting it.
story:
Iris sat in a big chair at the salon. Grandma stood right beside her. Iris wanted her hair to look pretty like Grandma's. But the hairdresser kept stopping! First she combed Iris's hair. Then she snipped once. Then she combed again. Snip. Again!

Why did she comb so much? Iris began to count. "One comb, one snip," said Iris. "Two combs, one snip." The comb made the hair lie flat and neat. Then the scissors could cut it straight. Iris watched the soft hairs fall. They floated down like little feathers.

A small piece of hair landed on a card on the counter. "Look, Grandma! A hair on my card!" Iris gave the card back to the hairdresser. Iris kicked her feet, happy in the big chair. Then she looked in the mirror. "Is that me?" she asked. Grandma smiled and said, "That is you, with your very first haircut."

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Taking turns means one person throws, and then the next person has a turn.
story:
Levi stood at the running track. The sun felt warm on his arms. A big hoop lay on the ground. A box of beanbags sat next to it. Levi wanted to throw every beanbag himself.

He picked up a beanbag. He threw it. It landed in the hoop. He grabbed another one. A kid named Mia reached for the box too. "More beanbags?" Levi wondered. Then he looked at Mia's hands. She had no beanbag at all.

Levi held one out. "Your turn," he said. Mia threw it. It missed the hoop. Then it was Levi's turn again. Throw, pass, throw, pass. His hands were learning the big ball next. Coach Maya rolled it to him. Levi caught it with both hands. The ball felt real and bumpy. "Again!" he said, and passed the ball back.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A referee watches the game and makes sure players follow the rules.
story:
Charles sat on the big couch. It was game morning at his house. Uncle Ben was there. Grandma was there. The neighbors came too. Everyone counted, "One, two, three, watch!"

The game started on TV. Charles saw a man in a striped shirt. The man ran back and forth. He kept watching the players. "Is he scary?" Charles asked. "No," said Uncle Ben. "Just watch what he does."

A player pushed another player. The striped man blew his whistle. He held up his hand. The game stopped. Then it started again.

"He watches the game," said Charles. "He made them stop!" Uncle Ben smiled. Grandma swept popcorn off the rug. The neighbors cheered. Charles waved his little flag. "One, two, three, watch!" he shouted, right along with everyone.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A power cut can make all the houses on a street go dark at once.
story:
The lights went out. The TV went out too. The whole room went dark.

"Mama!" Leo called.

"I am here," said Mama. She lit a candle with a match. The flame tickled the air. Then the room had a little glow.

Leo looked out the window. The street was dark. The neighbor's house was dark. The big house at the corner was dark too.

"All dark!" said Leo. "Every house!"

"Yes," said Mama. "The power went out on our street."

Leo clapped his hands. "We are a dark team!"

Mama laughed. "A big dark team, all up and down the street."

They sat close on the rug. The candle made shadows on the wall. Leo put his hand up. The shadow got big.

"Look! My hand makes a giant!" said Leo.

Mama moved the candle. The giant grew tall. Then it got small.

Soon the lights came back on. The TV hummed. The street glowed out the window, house by house.

"It's early bedtime," said Mama. She blew out the candle. The smoke curled up like a little worm.

"Good night, candle," said Leo.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Freshly fallen snow is white.
story:
Gabriel woke up at Grandma's house. He looked out the big window. Snow had fallen in the night. The snow was white. The fence was red. The bird feeder was blue.

"I want to draw the snow," said Gabriel. Grandma gave him white paper and crayons. Gabriel drew the red fence. He drew the blue bird feeder. He drew a green pine tree. Then he picked the white crayon. He drew and drew. But nothing showed up. The white snow did not show on the white paper. Gabriel made a sad face.

"Try this," said Grandma. She gave him a blue piece of paper. Gabriel drew with the white crayon again. The snow showed up! It looked soft and puffy. He drew white snow on the blue roof. He drew white snow on the green tree. Grandma clapped her hands.

"It looks like a map of the yard," she said. Gabriel smiled. He took his drawing to the window. He gave a little wave to the red fence. Then Grandma brought warm pretzels. They were a little salty. Gabriel ate one and watched the white snow fall. "More snow," he said. "More blue paper too."

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: Big brothers and sisters wash their hands before holding a new baby.
story:
Luca sat in the family car. He was going to meet his new baby sister. "One baby, two big hands," said Daddy. "My hands will hold her," said Luca. He had been playing in the yard. His hands had mud on them. One, two, three little brown spots.

The car stopped. Mommy carried the baby in a soft blanket. Luca ran to her. "My turn!" he said. He held out his muddy hands. Mommy shook her head. She pointed to the sink.

Luca turned the faucet. The water ran over his hands. The mud washed away. One, two, three spots gone. Then he counted his clean fingers. One to ten.

Mommy put the baby in his arms. The baby had a tiny nose. She made a small sound. Luca stroked her soft blanket. "I washed," he whispered. The baby grabbed his finger. She held on tight.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: A backpack is a bag you carry on your back.
story:
Asher stood by the school gate. His backpack was very big. It was full of toys.

Asher tried to walk to the door. His backpack was too heavy. He fell down on the slippery grass. His toys rolled out everywhere.

A big truck went by. It came from the farm. It honked its horn. Asher's toy cow jumped. It landed in the truck! The truck stopped.

The driver got out. She picked up the cow. "This belongs to you," she said. She put it in Asher's hand.

Asher sat on the step. He opened his backpack. He took out his toy train. He took out his robot. He took out his ball. Now the backpack was light.

He put it on his back. He could walk fast! He could even run to the door. His backpack bounced up and down.

His teacher waved at the gate. Asher waved back. Inside, he saw a surprise. The toy cow sat on the desk, waiting for him.

"How did you get here?" Asher asked. The cow just smiled.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Saying "sorry" is a way to show you know you hurt someone.
story:
Charlie was playing blocks with her friend Sam. Sam built a tall tower. It had a red block on top.

Charlie reached for a blue block. Her elbow bumped the tower. Crash! All the blocks fell down.

Sam looked at the blocks. His mouth went flat and sad. "My tower," he said.

Mom came over. She sat on the floor with them. "What can we say?" she asked softly.

Charlie thought hard. Was there a word for this? "Sorry," she said. "Sorry, Sam."

Sam's mouth went up again. "It's okay. Want to build it with me?"

Charlie nodded. She handed Sam the red block. Then she found a funny green block with a bumpy side. "Can this go on top?" she asked.

"Yes!" said Sam. "You put it on."

They took turns. Charlie placed one block. Then Sam placed one block. The new tower grew tall, taller, tallest of all.

Mom clapped her hands. "Lunch soon," she said. "First, let's put the blocks in the basket."

Charlie put in three blocks. Sam put in three blocks. The basket filled up, one handful at a time.

"Same for you, same for me," said Sam.

Charlie smiled. "Let's leave the red one out," she said. "For after lunch."

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: Letters can be written as big capital letters or small lowercase letters.
story:
Zoey put on her red sweater for school. She loved letter time. The wall had big letters. A big A hung up high.

The teacher read a book about a fish. "Look," said Zoey. "A little circle with a tail." She pointed at the small a. "That is not A. A is big."

Her friend Sam smiled. "Trace it," he said. Zoey traced the small a with her finger. Then she looked up at the big A. She traced that one too.

"Same letter!" said Zoey. "Big A. Small a. Same, same!" She clapped her hands.

The teacher read on. "The fish can swim fast." Zoey found the small f. Then she found the big F on the wall. "Same letter," she said. "F says ffff, like fish."

Sam clapped too. "You found it," he said.

Zoey turned the page. She pointed at a beautiful blue whale. "W," she said. "Big W or small w. Same letter." She smiled and read on, "Whales can swim in the sea."

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: If you lose something in a busy place, you tell your grown-up instead of going to search by yourself.
story:
Willow wanted her bunny. Bunny was not on her bed. Bunny was not in the toy box.

Willow ran for the big hall. It was full of bags from the market. She wanted to look behind all the bags. Then she stopped. She went back to the kitchen instead.

"Mama, bunny is lost," said Willow. Mama wiped her hands on a towel. "Let us look together," said Mama. They peeked in the bags. No bunny. They looked under the sofa. Willow heard a little scratch under there. Mama reached in and pulled out bunny, with a yucky bit of dust on one ear.

Mama washed the ear with a warm cloth. Willow hugged bunny tight. "We found her together," said Willow.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: Writing your name on your things helps them find their way back to you.
story:
Blake marched down the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her lunchbox tight. The hall smelled like crayons and floor wax. Her new shoes went squeak, squeak.

At lunch, a boy had a lunchbox just like hers. Red, with a dog on it. A huge mix-up! "Is this mine or yours?" Blake asked. The boy looked at his lid. "This one says Sam," he said.

Blake opened her box. Her name was inside the lid. Mom had written it there. Blake took her box and Sam took his. At home time, another kid found her dropped hat on the floor. He read the name tag. He ran it to her. Blake smiled and waved. "Thanks," she said.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Pockets in a coat can hold small things like mittens.
story:
Wren put on her red coat all by herself. She pushed one arm in. She pushed the other arm in. The coat was on.

Now came the zipper. Wren held the little tab. She pushed it up, up, up. It stopped halfway. She pulled it back down. Then she pushed it up again, slowly. This time it went all the way to the top. "I did it!" said Wren.

Mama was making lunch at the stove. "Can I help?" asked Wren. "You can set the mittens by the door," said Mama. Wren ran to get her mittens. But one mitten slipped out of her hand. It slid under the chair. Wren found it again. Then she saw her coat pocket. She tucked one mitten in. She tucked the other mitten in. Both mittens sat snug and safe.

At lunch, Wren ate her sandwich. After lunch, she remembered her mittens. She opened the pocket. There they were, both together. She pulled them out and waved them. "My mittens were hiding in my pretty red coat!"

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Carry a pencil with the point facing down so it cannot poke anyone.
story:
Victor went to the school library with his class. He saw a little table with paper and pencils. The teacher, Miss Ana, smiled at him.

"Today you will write your name," she said.

Victor picked up a pencil. He held it up high and waved it as he walked to his chair. Then he remembered. Miss Ana had shown them. The point goes down. He turned the pencil around. Now the point faced the floor. "Point down," he said to himself. "Point down."

He sat down and held the pencil the right way. He pressed it on the paper. A little line came out. He made a big V. Then an i, then a c, then more letters. He looked at his paper.

"I did it!" said Victor. "That is my name!"

Miss Ana clapped her hands. "It says Victor," she said.

Victor was not sad anymore. Writing was fun. He wrote his name again. Then he wrote it one more time. He carried his paper to the shelf, point down, all the way.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Crayons can melt if they are left in a hot car on a sunny day.
story:
Charles went to the art studio with his mama. He wanted to draw a big sun. He looked for his crayons. "Where are my crayons?" he asked.

"We left them in the car," said Mama. "I will get them." She went out to the hot, sunny car. She came back with the box. Charles opened the box. He picked up a red crayon. It felt soft. It bent like a noodle!

Charles tried to draw. The soft crayon made a fat, shiny line. It smeared and smeared. "Oh no," said Charles. "My sun will not look right." He tried again. The red crayon bent more. It left shiny red smudges on the paper.

Then Charles had an idea. He pressed the soft crayon gently. It made a round dot. He pressed the yellow one too. It made a round dot. He mixed the red dots and yellow dots with his finger. Now his sun looked round and orange and shiny!

"Look, Mama!" said Charles. "My soft crayons make dots!" He made dots all along the edge of his sun. Dot, dot, dot. They looked like the sun's rays. The teacher hung the picture on the studio wall.

"I like hot car crayons," said Charles. He made one more shiny dot on the corner of his page.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In ice hockey, players use sticks to hit a flat disc called a puck.
story:
Addison sat with her family at the restaurant. A big screen glowed on the wall. Everyone was watching an ice hockey game. Addison wanted to see the ball. She looked and looked. "I can't find the ball," she said.

Then she saw it. The players hit a small black disc with their sticks. It slid fast on the smooth ice. The disc was not a ball at all. It was flat, like a little pancake. "That's not a ball," Addison said. Her dad smiled and nodded. "They call it a puck," he said.

Addison watched the puck zoom and spin. A player hit it hard with his stick. The puck flew into the net. The crowd on the screen cheered. The restaurant filled with happy shouts. Addison clapped her hands.

Later, the waiter brought a plate of warm bread. Addison dipped a piece in the little dish of soup. She took a bite and smiled at her root vegetable soup. Then she pointed at the screen. "Puck!" she said. The puck slid by again, fast and smooth.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A triangle has three sides and three corners.
story:
Ibrahim sat at the art table. He wanted to make a house out of paper. He had a red square. He had a brown rectangle. But the roof was missing.

"What shape is a roof?" he asked. "A triangle," said his friend Mia. The teacher gave them bread and cheese. She cut the bread with a safe knife. Ibrahim watched from his seat. Each piece came out pointy. "Triangles!" yelled Mia.

Ibrahim picked up his triangle sandwich. He touched the pointy parts. "One, two, three," he counted. Three corners. He turned the bread over. "One, two, three." Still three corners. He took a big bite. Now the corner was gone. He counted again. "One, two, three." The other side still had three.

Then Ibrahim knew what to do. He drew a triangle for the roof. One side, two sides, three sides. He glued it on top of his square house. Mia gave him a spoon of glue when his pot ran low. "Thank you," said Ibrahim. The house had a square, a rectangle, and a triangle on top. "One, two, three corners," said Ibrahim. "Perfect roof!"

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Hanging your coat on a hook keeps it off the floor.
story:
John dropped his coat on the hall floor. Then he ran to see Grandpa's toy frog. The frog hopped when you pushed it. "Hop, frog, hop!" said John. The frog made a loud click every time.

Later, John wanted to go outside. "Where is my coat?" he said. He looked under the table. He looked behind the big chair. No coat. He looked at the coat pile on the floor. "That is not mine," he said. Then Grandma held up a coat. "Is this it?" It was John's coat, all dusty from the floor. "Silly coat," said John. He laughed.

The next day, John put his coat on by himself. One arm in. Other arm in. Then the zipper. Up, up, up it went. "I did it!" he said. Grandpa clapped. At the door, John saw a little hook on the wall. He hung his coat right on it. The coat stayed up, off the floor. "Look, Grandpa! My coat can stand on the wall!" said John. Grandpa laughed. "So it can," he said.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: On a tablet, you tap the screen with your finger to choose things.
story:
Lena wanted to draw a sun at school. Teacher Sam held up a tablet. "You can draw on this," he said.

Lena pressed her whole hand on the screen. The screen stayed dark. She pressed harder. Still dark. Her friend Max slid the tablet over to her. "Try your finger," he said.

Lena lifted one finger. She tapped the screen, tap, tap. The screen lit up bright. "It works!" she said. She tapped the little yellow sun icon and the drawing app opened. She drew a big yellow sun with red rays.

Then the teacher rang the little bell. Time to clean up. Lena tapped the button and the drawing went away. She put the tablet back on the shelf, flat and neat.

Max looked for his tablet plug. Lena pointed to it on the wall. "There it is," she said. Max smiled. Then Lena tapped his screen too. It lit up for him.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours.
story: Paint day was here. Charlotte ran to the art table. She wanted to paint a rainbow. But there were only three paint pots. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue. Charlotte frowned. "How can I paint a rainbow?" she asked. She looked at the pots. Then she looked at the open window. A dog barked outside, and a boy laughed. Charlotte got a brush. She dabbed red. She dabbed yellow. Then she mixed them. Orange! She gasped. She tried blue and yellow. Green! She tried red and blue. Purple! Charlotte painted her rainbow. It had red, yellow, blue, orange, green and purple. She held it up high. "Look at my rainbow!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Tomorrow is the day after today.
story:
Jasper stood by his bed. The sky outside was dark. He wanted to see Ben now.

"Can we go to Ben's house now?" he asked.

"Not now," said Mama. "Ben is sleeping. You will go tomorrow."

Jasper frowned. "I want to go today."

"You played today," said Mama. "Today is almost done. Tomorrow comes after you sleep."

Jasper got into bed. He held his bear. He counted his sleepy things. One bear. Two socks. Three small cars on the shelf.

First the room went dark. Then it went quiet. Jasper kept his eyes closed. He slept and slept.

Then light came in the window. Jasper opened his eyes. "Is it tomorrow now?" he asked.

"Yes," said Mama. "It is tomorrow."

Jasper jumped up. He put on his socks. He said sorry to his bear for leaving him. "The teacher will not mind," said Mama. "You can bring the bear too."

They went out the door. The sun was up. "Ben!" said Jasper. "I slept, and now it is tomorrow!"

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: Wrapping paper hides a present, so nobody can see what is inside until it is opened.
story:
Liam turned three today. The party was at the park. There was cake on a big table. Grandma held his hand.

A big box sat under the tree. It had blue paper with stars. "Is it for me?" Liam asked. "It is for you," said Daddy. "But not yet."

Liam picked up the box. He shook it. Something went bump, bump. He squeezed it. He held it up to his ear. "Is it a ball?" he asked. "Maybe," said Mama with a smile. "Is it a farm set?" asked Liam. "You will see," said Grandma.

Liam could not see inside. The paper hid everything. He turned the box all around. Still no peek. "This is tricky," he said. Everyone laughed.

At last it was time. Daddy helped him pull the paper off. Rip, rip, rip! Inside was a little farm. There was a cow and a sheep. "I can feed the sheep," said Liam. He hugged the box. "It was a farm all along!"

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away.
story:
Grayson set his teddy bear in a red boot. "You are in a boat!" he said. The bear sailed across the rug. Then the boat bumped into a pot from the pretend kitchen. Crash! The pot rolled and spoons fell out. What a mess!

His friend Mia came to play. "We can play house," said Grayson. Mia stirred the pot. "Soup for bear!" she said. Grayson patted the bear. "Time for sleep," he said softly. But then Mom called, "Time to go, Mia!" Grayson looked at the big mess on the rug. "Wait," he said. He put the spoons in the pot. He put the pot in the kitchen. Mia put the bear in the boat, and the boat on the shelf. "There," said Grayson. "All done playing, all clean." He waved at the shelf. "Bye, bear. Sleep alone now." Then he held Mia's hand, and they ran to the door.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: We ask before we take something that belongs to someone else.
story:
Jaxon ran to the sandbox at the park. He saw a boy there with a bright red truck. The boy was pushing it up and down. "Beep, beep," the boy said. Jaxon wanted that truck so much.

Jaxon grabbed the truck fast. The boy's face went sad. He began to cry. Jaxon looked at the truck in his hands. Then he looked at the boy's sad face. What made the crying start? Jaxon wondered.

Jaxon gave the truck back. He held out his hand. "Truck, please?" he asked. The boy stopped crying. He smiled. "Okay," he said. "You can have a turn." Jaxon pushed the truck. "Beep, beep," he said.

Then Jaxon saw a puddle near the swings. A turtle sat by the water. "Look, turtle!" Jaxon said. The turtle slid in with a splash. Splash, splash, went the water. "Did the turtle make the splash?" Jaxon asked.

The boy came over too. They jumped in the puddle together. Splash, splash! Jaxon fell down, but he was okay. "You are strong," said the boy. Jaxon laughed.

Then it was time to go home. "Bye, bye," said the boy. Jaxon waved. "Truck again tomorrow?" he asked. The boy nodded. "Yes, truck again tomorrow."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: People often wear special clothes to a celebration.
story:
Madeline woke up early. Today was the big family party. She could not pick what to wear. She held up her blue shirt. She held up her brown pants. None of them felt right for a party.

Mom came in with a soft red dress. "Grandma wore this when she was little," Mom said. Madeline touched the shiny fabric. She put it on and looked in the mirror. The dress made her feel like a party was coming. Dad put on his best long shirt too. Even Baby Sam had a tiny white cap.

Downstairs, the house smelled like warm bread. Grandma lit the candles, and Madeline watched from her chair. Everyone sat down together in their special clothes. Madeline smiled at her big cousin. "You look like a princess," he said. Grandma touched Madeline's cheek. "Our little Madeline," she said. Outside the sky looked stormy, but inside everyone was warm. Madeline wiggled her loose tooth and giggled. Then Grandma said, "Time to eat!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A day goes from morning, to afternoon, to evening, to night.
story:
Milo loved the class rabbit. He fed her every morning. But today he wanted to paint her picture, and painting time came later, after nap.

The room got dark and quiet. Milo slept on his little mat. When he woke up, he saw the sun through the window. "It is morning now," he said. "I missed my turn!"

His teacher, a kind woman with loose gray hair, shook her head. "It is afternoon now," she said. "A day goes from morning, to afternoon, to evening, to night. After nap, it is afternoon."

Milo looked outside. The sun was low, not high. So it was not morning. He had not missed anything at all.

"Painting time is now," the teacher said. Milo ran to the easel. He paid close attention to the rabbit's long ears. He drew one ear, then the other.

Tomorrow he would paint her again. "I will use pink," he said, "for her nose."

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A cube, like a toy block, has six flat faces, and each one is a square.
story:
Gabriella sat at the art table. She wanted to make a house for her toy rabbit. She drew a square for one wall. She drew a rectangle for the door. She drew a triangle for the roof. Then she drew a big circle for a window.

But the paper house would not stand up. It flopped over. The rabbit slid off onto the floor. "Try my block," said her friend Milo. He gave her a wooden block.

Gabriella put a sticker on one face of the block. It was a square sticker on a square face. She turned the block over. She put a sticker there, too. She turned it again and again. Sticker, turn, sticker, turn. She counted one, two, three, four, five, six. Six faces. Six stickers. Every face was a square, just like her square sticker.

"Your rabbit has a house now," said Milo. "It can sit on top." Gabriella set the rabbit on the clean wooden block. The rabbit did not fall. It stood still and tall. "Welcome home," said Gabriella.
